q7.answer: L4 does everything in one transaction. It locks the enrollment row, checks the code against the pending secret, and upserts user_totp with the new sealed secret, last_step set to the matched step and confirmed_at. It then deletes the enrollment row, deletes all old recovery codes and inserts 10 new hashes, deletes every other session of the user except the current sid, and deletes the user's pending_logins rows. If anything fails before the commit, all of it rolls back: the old secret, old codes and other sessions stay as they were. The plaintext codes are shown only after the commit, and if that page is lost the user runs L1 and L4 again.

q8.answer: It is a pending_logins row (sha256 token_hash, user_id, expires_at 5 minutes after S4, failures). The browser refers to it with the mfa_pending cookie, which holds the raw new_token(32) and is httponly, secure, samesite=Lax, max_age=300 and path=/login. The row is deleted when: S7 or S8 succeeds; the 5th wrong entry or expiry happens (S6, and an expired row is also deleted when it is read); a new password sign-in for the same user replaces it; L4 confirm or L6 disable runs; the periodic cleanup job runs; or the user is deleted (CASCADE).

q9.answer: The confirmed secret is in user_totp.secret_sealed, encrypted with seal(). A setup in progress is a separate totp_enrollments row with its own sealed secret and a 15-minute expires_at. Replay protection is user_totp.last_step. Recovery codes are rows in recovery_codes, holding the sha256 of the normalised code and a nullable used_at. 2FA is on exactly when a user_totp row exists for the user.

q10.answer: Sign-in reads only user_totp, which keeps the old secret until L4 swaps it, and it never reads totp_enrollments. So during a replacement, sign-in still needs a code from the old secret or an unused recovery code. If the user abandons the replacement, cancel deletes the enrollment row, or it counts as missing after 15 minutes. Either way the old secret and recovery codes stay unchanged and the account is back to On.

q11.answer: An entry of exactly 6 digits is checked as an authenticator code. Anything else is uppercased, stripped of spaces and hyphens, and checked as a recovery code. Yes, an unknown or already-used recovery code is a wrong entry: it increments failures like any other wrong entry and counts toward the limit of 5.
